ISDS have been around for 2 decades now and from my VERY limited point of view they seem like a necessary evil in today's economy. Imagine I invest in X industry in a foreign country, but future political changes mandate to expropriate assets or prevent me from withdrawing my capital (this has happened in Venezuela I believe but don't quote me on that). In this case an ISDS makes sense, especially for countries with a GDP heavily dependent on foreign investment, like Mexico, in which the last thing you need is create investor panic. However, they are a double-edge sword since, as a nation, you have to watch closely your future political agenda in order to not transgress agreements on previous investments... but again, your GDP depends substantially on foreign investment anyways. To me it seems a prudent decision for any country in development to increase internal markets and decrease foreign investment dependency.

Moreover, I just saw the video of Bernie Sanders talking about trade agreements between the US and countries like China and Mexico. As a person that has worked at sweatshops, most notably Foxconn, I can only tell that Bernie is right but I do not know what the implications to the global market would be if manufacturing came back to the US. For example, Foxconn has a manufacturing plant in Juarez, Mexico that produces ~50k Dell computers a day. Over 6k jobs were created in that city alone with millions invested in it. At this point, bringing back those jobs would mean a big blow to Mexico (if you count Ford, HP, IBM, etc..) with higher poverty rates and more likely increased immigration to the US, an investment loss for these companies, and an advantage to other brands that are based in other low-income countries. To me it seems that consumer responsibility would always be the best approach, and even coordinated investor-activism, but then again, I am not a politician, nor an attorney, nor an economist so please discuss alternatives on this issue because it seems complicated to me.
